explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The man measures the room next to the inner sanctuary at twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, and then he says to Ezekiel, "This is the Most Holy Place." (Ezekiel 41:4) Notice it's a perfect square. I like a tidy room.

Close, because priests do show up later in this passage. But that's not what the man calls this room. Right after he measures it, he says, "This is the Most Holy Place." (Ezekiel 41:4) The chambers for the priests come later, in chapter 42.

I get the guess, since the man has been measuring pillars all over this section. Side pillars are in the verses just before (Ezekiel 41:1-3). But when he gets to this room, he tells Ezekiel, "This is the Most Holy Place." (Ezekiel 41:4) The pillars are just the warm-up act, friend.

explanations.answer: The table that is before the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The wooden altar is three cubits high and two cubits square, and the man tells Ezekiel, "This is the table that is before the LORD." (Ezekiel 41:22) Altar and table in one verse, so don't worry if your head did a little spin. I think a table is a good place to be when you're before the LORD.

The ark is a famous name, so I see why it jumped out. But this verse never mentions it. What the man says about the wooden altar is, "This is the table that is before the LORD." (Ezekiel 41:22) The ark isn't named anywhere in this passage.

explanations.answer: The mercy seat of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's another well-known name, friend, but it's not the one here. Ezekiel sees an altar of wood, and the man tells him, "This is the table that is before the LORD." (Ezekiel 41:22) The passage doesn't use the words mercy seat anywhere. So we stick with the table.

That's right, baker. The man says these are the holy chambers "…where the priests who approach the LORD will eat the most holy offerings." (Ezekiel 42:13) So the chambers are for priests, and the offerings are eaten right there. Grain offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings are all named in that verse.

Elders are a good guess, but this verse isn't about them. The man says these are the holy chambers where "…the priests who approach the LORD will eat the most holy offerings." (Ezekiel 42:13) The word is priests, friend. Nobody else gets named for these chambers.

I love a good singer, but my own voice cracks when I hum to the oven. Singers aren't in this verse, though. The man says the chambers are where "…the priests who approach the LORD will eat the most holy offerings." (Ezekiel 42:13) Priests are who these rooms are for.

True, baker. The man says the priests will place the most holy offerings there, "…for the place is holy." (Ezekiel 42:13) The grain offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings are all named. The text gives the reason right in the verse, so I don't have to guess.

It's actually true. The man does say the most holy offerings will be placed in these chambers, and he gives the reason: "…for the place is holy." (Ezekiel 42:13) The verse names the grain offerings, the sin offerings and the guilt offerings. So the reason is right there in the text, friend.

Not quite, friend. The man says the opposite. Once the priests have entered the holy area, "…they must not go out into the outer court until they have left behind the garments in which they minister…" (Ezekiel 42:14) So the garments stay behind, and the priests change first.

Right, baker. The man says the priests "…must not go out into the outer court until they have left behind the garments in which they minister, for these are holy." (Ezekiel 42:14) So they can't just stroll out wearing them. The garments stay, and other clothes go on.
That's it, baker. The man says the priests must leave the garments behind "…for these are holy." (Ezekiel 42:14) The reason is right there in the verse. Holy garments stay in the holy place.

That would be a good reason in my kitchen, where my apron has seen things. But the text gives a different one. The priests leave the garments behind "…for these are holy." (Ezekiel 42:14) Washing never comes up, friend.

explanations.answer: Because those garments belong to the high priest
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but the verse never mentions a high priest. It says the priests must leave behind the garments in which they minister, "…for these are holy." (Ezekiel 42:14) That's the whole reason the text gives. Holy is the word to remember.

Yes, baker. The man says the priests "…are to put on other clothes before they approach the places that are for the people." (Ezekiel 42:14) So there's a change of clothes between the holy area and the people. Simple as that.

Levites are a good guess, friend, but they aren't in this verse. The man says the priests put on other clothes "…before they approach the places that are for the people." (Ezekiel 42:14) The word is people. The man doesn't name anybody else.

A prince is a fancy guess, but this verse says something plainer. The priests put on other clothes "…before they approach the places that are for the people." (Ezekiel 42:14) People is the word, baker.

explanations.answer: To separate the holy from the common
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. After all that measuring, the text says the wall was there "…to separate the holy from the common." (Ezekiel 42:20) Five hundred cubits long and five hundred cubits wide, with a wall all the way around. The text tells us what the wall is for, so no guessing needed.

explanations.answer: To keep enemy armies from getting in
explanations.explanation: A wall makes you think of armies, I know. But the text gives a different reason, and it doesn't mention enemies at all. The wall was there "…to separate the holy from the common." (Ezekiel 42:20) That's the purpose the verse gives, friend.

explanations.answer: To mark where the city's edge begins
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible guess, but the verse doesn't say anything about a city's edge. The man measures the area on all four sides, and the wall is there "…to separate the holy from the common." (Ezekiel 42:20) That's the job the text gives it. Holy on one side, common on the other.
